Superfluous
sū-pĕr'flōō-ŭs
adj. (having something in excess; in the law, a beast or a man with a member overgrown or malformed, disqualified from the altar or the priesthood)
Latin superfluus, overflowing, from super, above, and fluere, to flow. In Leviticus the word covers any part in excess, as lacking covers any part deficient.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The law of the priesthood lists the disqualifying blemishes and includes “a blind man, or a lame, or he that hath a flat nose, or any thing superfluous” (Lev 21:18). The law of the offerings applies the same standard to the animal: a bullock or lamb “that hath any thing superfluous or lacking in his parts” may be offered for a freewill offering, “but for a vow it shall not be accepted” (Lev 22:23). Two things must be said carefully. First, this is not a judgment on the worth of the disabled man. The blemished priest was not cast out of Israel and not cut off from the sanctuary's benefits — the very next verse provides that he shall eat the bread of his God, both of the most holy and of the holy (Lev 21:22). He was barred from officiating, not from belonging. Second, the whole standard exists to say something about the Priest who was coming: holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners, without blemish and without spot. Paul then uses the same adjective in an entirely ordinary sense: “as touching the ministering to the saints, it is superfluous for me to write to you” (2Co 9:1) — unnecessary, because their willingness was already known.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines superfluous as more than is wanted; unnecessary; useless; and, of a part, exceeding what is natural or requisite.

expand to see more

SUPERFLUOUS, a. More than is wanted, or is sufficient; rendering more than enough; unnecessary; useless.

2. Unnecessary; not required by the circumstances of the case.

In Scripture, of a member exceeding what is natural, and so disqualifying for the priesthood or the altar.

Key Scripture

Lev 21:18 — "For whatsoever man he be that hath a blemish, he shall not approach: a blind man, or a lame, or he that hath a flat nose, or any thing superfluous,"

Lev 22:23 — "Either a bullock or a lamb that hath any thing superfluous or lacking in his parts, that mayest thou offer for a freewill offering; but for a vow it shall not be accepted."

1Pe 1:19 — "But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot:"

Modern Corruption

The blemish laws are read either as ancient cruelty toward the disabled or as a warrant for judging people by their bodies, and Leviticus 21:22 refutes both in a single verse.

expand to see more

Leviticus 21 is regularly produced as evidence that the God of the Old Testament despised the disabled, and the charge is answered inside the chapter itself. The blemished son of Aaron did not lose his priestly standing, his inheritance, his family, or his access to God. Verse 22 is explicit: he shall eat the bread of his God, both of the most holy, and of the holy. He was excluded from one thing only — the act of officiating at the altar — and he was excluded for the same reason a lamb with anything superfluous or lacking was excluded from a vow offering: because everything at that altar was a picture, and the picture had to be exact. The whole apparatus was pointing at one unblemished Priest offering one unblemished Lamb, and a marred symbol would have preached a marred gospel. The opposite abuse is worse and appears within the church: the use of these chapters as a general licence to weigh people by their bodies, their appearance, or their capacities. James 2 forbids it outright, the Lord chose the weak things and the base things and the things that are despised, and 2 Corinthians 12 puts the apostolic ministry itself in a body with a thorn. Israel's altar required perfection because Christ was coming; the church requires faith because He has come.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew sarua' (H8311), stretched out, deformed by excess; qalat (H7038), stunted, lacking; mum (H3971), a blemish; Greek perissos (G4053), abundant, superfluous.

expand to see more

Hebrew sarua' (H8311) — extended, overgrown, having a member in excess; Leviticus 21:18, 22:23.

Hebrew mum (H3971) — a blemish, a spot; the disqualifying mark on priest or victim, and denied of the Servant; Leviticus 21:17-21, Daniel 1:4.

Greek perissos (G4053) — over and above, more than enough; Paul's ordinary use in the collection chapters; 2 Corinthians 9:1.

Usage

"“Or any thing superfluous” — the blemish list for the priesthood."

"“Superfluous or lacking in his parts” — excess and deficiency alike disqualify a vow offering."

"“It is superfluous for me to write to you” — Paul's ordinary sense: unnecessary."
